name: Fasting from dopamine (screen fast)

lead: Fasting from dopamine, also called dopamine detoxing, means abstaining for a set period from phones, social media, gaming, snacking and similar impulsive habits. In looksmaxxing circles it is discussed as a way to cut compulsive scrolling and reclaim time and attention.

The appearance link is indirect: time and willpower freed from screens can go to sleep, exercise, grooming and skin routines. The method was introduced by psychologist Cameron Sepah as a cognitive behavioural approach to impulsive behaviour, and some experts have criticised the neurochemical framing.

paras: People typically pick a block of hours or days, put away phones and other screens, and substitute lower-stimulation activities such as reading, walking or exercise. Definitions vary: some limit it to online technology, others also avoid work, talking or exercise.

There are no direct physical risks in screen abstinence, though more extreme versions (avoiding food, speech or social contact) have drawn criticism from clinicians such as Peter Grinspoon as ascetic and unhealthy.

chain: More sleep, training and grooming consistency
angle.text: A screen fast does not change appearance itself. Proponents use it to clear time and attention for the routines that do, such as exercise, sleep and skincare.

lead: Dopamine fasting, or dopamine detoxing, is the practice of temporarily abstaining from impulsive and behavioural habits such as smartphone and social media use, emotional eating, gaming, gambling, shopping and pornography. Wikipedia describes it as developed by California psychologist Cameron Sepah as a form of cognitive behavioural therapy. [1]

For people working on their looks, the appeal is practical. Time previously spent scrolling can be redirected to training, sleep and grooming, and proponents describe less anxiety and better self-control as side benefits. [1]

Sepah has said the goal is not literally to lower dopamine but to reduce impulsive responses to cues, such as reaching for a phone. Neuroscientists such as Ciara McCabe have criticised the idea that the brain can be 'reset' by avoiding dopamine triggers. [1] The phrase spread through 2019 and 2020 media coverage, including The New York Times and Vice. [1]
infobox: Screen-only fast; broader abstinence from stimulation

paras: There is no fixed definition. Some people restrict only online technology, while others also avoid work, exercise, physical contact and unnecessary conversation; the extreme version is sensory deprivation. [1]
Sepah frames it as targeting the behaviours dopamine rewards, not dopamine levels themselves. [1]

Claimed benefits include more self-discipline, less anxiety, quitting bad habits and more time for healthier ones such as exercise. A New York Times writer reported that her subject found everyday life more exciting and fun. [1]

Critics say dopamine is essential and that removing a stimulus does not lower dopamine in the body. McCabe called the reset idea nonsense, and Grinspoon wrote that the aim should be managing impulses rather than eliminating them, criticising increasingly ascetic versions. [1]

No studies found testing screen fasting as a looks intervention. Wikipedia lists related work: a 2022 Lifestyle Medicine paper by Fei and colleagues examining dopamine fasting as a possible intervention for behavioural addiction, and a 2024 Computers in Human Behavior study by Zheng and colleagues linking higher screen time with impulsivity in adults aged 30-45. [1]
